stories.headline: Update: Fed Holds Rates at 3.75%-4% in 10-2 Vote as Warsh Cites Inflation, Announces Smaller Meeting Schedule
stories.summary:
The Federal Reserve left its benchmark federal funds rate unchanged at a range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent on Wednesday, at its last meeting before the midterm elections. The Federal Open Market Committee voted 10-2, with two members dissenting in favor of a quarter-point increase. The decision follows a September hike, the central bank's first in three years, and inflation remains above 3 percent.

Chair Kevin Warsh told reporters that politics played no role in the pause and said an "information-rich" period before the December meeting will help officials decide their next step. He repeated his pledge to bring inflation down and deliver price stability, "no ifs, ands or buts." Investors widely expect another increase in December, according to coverage from several outlets.

Warsh also said the committee will phase in an adjusted meeting schedule, voting at seven of its eight meetings next year and six in 2028, with one meeting devoted to broad strategy. The new development today is the formal rate decision, the dissent pattern and the schedule change, going beyond the pre-meeting expectations previously reported.

The rate level is among the highest going into a midterm election in more than 20 years. Inflation and the cost of living are central issues in the closing campaign, and Democrats and Republicans have each sought to frame the economy to their advantage.

stories.headline: Trump Demands Peltola Be Barred From Alaska Senate Race After Report on Namesake Candidate
stories.summary:
President Trump said Wednesday that Democrat Mary Peltola should not be allowed to run for Senate in Alaska and should be prosecuted, after a New York Times report that operatives aligned with her campaign recruited candidates to peel votes from Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. One of them, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., shares nearly the same name as the incumbent and will appear on the ballot. Trump called for last-minute changes to the ballot.

Peltola's campaign had for months denied any connection to the namesake candidate. A group called Alaskans for Mary said it "has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign." Republicans have condemned the arrangement as a ploy to split the vote and confuse voters.

The Justice Department has sued over the ballot arrangement. Legal scholars say the suit faces hurdles, including whether anonymous ballot analysis can prove voter confusion, and some conservative commentators have said it lacks a clear legal basis. Democrats and some election-law experts view the push for late changes with skepticism, noting that early voting is under way.

The dispute comes less than a week before Election Day, in a race that could help decide Senate control. Early-voting trends and polls show a difficult environment for Republicans nationally, with several tight Senate contests.

stories.headline: HHS to Allow Compounding of Unapproved Peptide Drugs Over FDA Staff Objections
stories.summary:
The Department of Health and Human Services said Wednesday it will allow compounding pharmacies to manufacture and sell peptides not yet on the list of approved substances. The notice says HHS will practice enforcement discretion, a unilateral step by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. that makes several injections promoted by online influencers widely available.

Reports from The New York Times and The Guardian say most Food and Drug Administration scientific staff opposed the plan and had limited input in drafting it, according to six people familiar with its development. The FDA had advised against the move.

Supporters, including advocates of the Make America Healthy Again agenda, say the change expands patient access to therapies that are championed by Kennedy and popular among wellness communities. Critics, including agency scientists, argue the products are unproven and that bypassing the review process raises safety concerns.

It is not yet clear how quickly pharmacies will begin offering the products, or whether the policy will face legal challenge or congressional scrutiny.

stories.headline: Dolores Huerta, Labor Leader Who Co-Founded United Farm Workers, Dies at 96
stories.summary:
Dolores Huerta, the labor organizer and civil rights figure who co-founded the United Farm Workers and coined the rallying cry "Sí, se puede," died Wednesday at 96, her family announced on her Instagram account. The family wrote that they were deeply saddened to announce her passing.

Huerta helped lead strikes and boycotts to improve conditions for workers in the nation's fruit and vegetable fields, and fought to expand rights for Hispanic Americans. She co-founded the organization that became the UFW with Cesar Chavez and later became an influential figure in Democratic politics.

In early 2026, she told The New York Times that she had been raped by Chavez decades earlier, a disclosure that reshaped public discussion of the movement's history and his legacy.

stories.headline: Update: Death Toll in Spain Train Crash Rises to at Least 68, Transport Minister Calls Signal Order 'Inexplicable'
stories.summary:
A high-speed passenger train rear-ended another near Toledo, south of Madrid, on Wednesday morning, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens more, officials said. It is one of the deadliest rail disasters in Spanish history. The toll is well above the figure of at least 30 reported earlier in the day.

Transport Minister Óscar Puente said traffic control operators told one train to continue its journey while another was stopped farther along the tracks, an instruction he called "inexplicable." Spain's rail authority Adif said the trains were operated by Renfe and Iryo, both running between Madrid and Seville. More than 500 passengers were aboard. Survivors described people thrown from a dining car, broken limbs and passengers piled on top of one another. Some climbed out of windows, and others were carried to a nearby field on makeshift stretchers.

It was the second fatal crash this year involving the same two operators. A January derailment and collision killed 46 people, and its official cause has not been released, though preliminary findings pointed to a broken rail. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez visited the scene, promised a thorough investigation and declared three days of mourning. "If there has been negligence, it will come to light," he said.

The crash comes about a month before Spain's national election and could become a campaign issue over the competence of Sánchez's left-wing government. Opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo expressed concern and said his Popular Party canceled all its campaign events.

stories.headline: New York Times Reports Peltola Campaign Operatives Helped Recruit Spoiler Candidates Against Sen. Dan Sullivan
stories.summary:
The New York Times reported Wednesday that operatives aligned with Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola, along with senior Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee officials, spent months recruiting candidates to split votes from Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska. One recruited candidate shares the incumbent's name, Dan J. Sullivan. The report describes what was allegedly a covert "ballot composition project."

Peltola's campaign had repeatedly denied any connection to the second candidate's campaign, and the new reporting undercuts that claim. Republicans say it bolsters their long-standing allegation that the namesake candidacy was designed to confuse voters. Some Democrats and legal scholars note that fielding candidates is generally lawful and that the question is whether voters were actually misled.

The Justice Department has sued over the ballot arrangement, but legal experts say it faces hurdles, including whether anonymous ballot analysis can prove voter confusion. National Review and other conservative outlets called the Times findings the world's least surprising scoop, while others questioned the legal basis of the federal suit.

The race is one of several tight contests that will decide Senate control, with election day on November 3. Axios reported that control of the chamber may be uncertain well into November because of close races and state-specific voting rules.

stories.headline: Boston University Study Estimates About 75% of Deceased NFL Players Had CTE
stories.summary:
A new study published Wednesday in JAMA Network Open estimates that about 75 percent of former NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 had evidence of chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE. The Boston-based research team examined estimated prevalence among 2,362 players who died over the 15-year period.

The researchers used statistical techniques to reach the estimate, which suggests the degenerative brain disease is far more widespread among professional football players than previously understood. CTE is linked to repeated head impacts and can be definitively diagnosed only after death.

The finding adds pressure on the league and on football at all levels over player safety. The study estimates prevalence rather than confirming diagnoses in every case, a limitation that will likely shape debate over how to interpret the figure.

stories.headline: Update: Netanyahu and Eisenkot Face Difficult Paths to Power as Neither Bloc Nears Majority
stories.summary:
Early results from Israel's general election show Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud emerging as the largest single party, performing better than widely predicted. His existing bloc of ultra-nationalist and ultra-Orthodox parties appears just short of a 61-seat majority in the 120-seat Knesset. Analysts caution the early count was skewed toward areas with strong right-wing support, and turnout exceeded 77%.

His main rival, former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, would struggle to assemble a majority without parties led by Israel's Arab minority, which equalled or exceeded their previous record number of seats on partial results. Most Jewish opposition parties pledged during the campaign not to work with Arab-majority lists, citing a lack of shared values, though Arab-led parties could become kingmakers if others were willing to join forces with them. Arab Israelis, about one-fifth of the population, appeared to turn out in unprecedented numbers. Netanyahu would need to persuade one of the smaller opposition parties to join his coalition.

Both leaders addressed supporters overnight and pledged to form the next government. Netanyahu said the right-wing bloc has "a clear, decisive majority among the Zionist public" but stopped short of declaring victory. Eisenkot said "the public has chosen change" and that Israelis voted against Netanyahu continuing as prime minister.

A large number of absentee ballots, mostly from soldiers, remain uncounted, so a clear picture of the final result is not expected for another day or two. Coalition negotiations are likely to be protracted given the fragmented system.

stories.headline: Update: Treasury Sanctions North Korean and Russian Nationals Over Alleged IT Worker Fraud Scheme
stories.summary:
The Treasury Department on Wednesday sanctioned 10 individuals and one entity involved in an alleged scheme to defraud American businesses and benefit the North Korean military. The department's Office of Foreign Assets Control named eight North Korean nationals and two Russian nationals.

OFAC accused the group of facilitating a government-run information technology scheme that generates stolen identities, fake resumes and fake IT employees who infiltrate legitimate U.S. businesses. Such operations are alleged to funnel earnings back to Pyongyang to support its military programs.

The action targets what U.S. officials describe as a sustained effort to use remote work arrangements to evade sanctions on North Korea. The sanctions typically freeze any U.S.-based assets of those designated and bar Americans from doing business with them. Companies hiring remote technology workers are likely to face continued pressure to verify identities more rigorously.

stories.headline: Tanzania Announces First Natural Gas Discovery in More Than a Decade
stories.summary:
Tanzania has announced a significant natural gas discovery in the Mnazi Bay area in the country's south, the first such find in a decade. Energy Minister Juma Homera attended a ceremony at the Kasa-1X ST2 well, jointly owned by state-owned Tanzania Petroleum Development Corporation and French oil firm Maurel & Prom.

The estimated 223 billion cubic feet of gas was called a "major milestone" for the country's small oil and gas sector. The well is expected to begin production early next month and is intended to boost domestic supplies. Tanzania already holds reserves of 57.54 trillion cubic feet.

Natural gas accounted for nearly 80% of Tanzania's electricity generation in 2024, according to government statistics. Homera said the find helps ensure reliable, clean and affordable energy as industrial demand grows. The country has also promoted compressed natural gas for vehicles, with some Tanzanians converting cars to dual-fuel systems for lower fuel costs.

stories.headline: Republicans Spend an Estimated $183 Million on Transgender-Focused Ads in Final Midterm Stretch
stories.summary:
Republicans have spent an estimated $183 million on television ads focused on transgender-related attacks against Democrats in the final phase of the midterm elections, according to AdImpact data provided to the Associated Press. The spending, through Oct. 25, produced about 217,000 spots and exceeds what Republicans spent on similar ads at the same point in 2024.

Republicans see the issue as a way to offset voter concerns about President Trump's leadership and the economy, including rising gasoline prices. Texas' Senate race has drawn the most, about $58 million, with heavy spending also in Ohio, Kansas, South Carolina, Iowa and Mississippi. Trump has emphasized the theme at rallies, citing what he calls a threat to children and men in women's sports. Republican pollster Chris Wilson said the issue works as a proxy for a candidate's broader values and judgment rather than as a top voting priority.

Critics, including Democrats, note that few Americans are directly affected by the policies at issue and that voters consistently say high prices are their chief concern. The spending is a test of whether a theme that worked in past elections can still be potent when the economy dominates voters' thinking. The election is less than a week away.

stories.headline: Federal Reserve Expected to Hold Rates Steady After September Hike, With Midterms Six Days Away
stories.summary:
The Federal Reserve is set to announce its interest rate decision at 2 p.m. ET on Wednesday, concluding its Oct. 27-28 meeting. Traders are pricing in roughly 90.6 percent odds that the central bank will hold rates steady, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool. The pause would follow last month's increase, the first rate hike since 2023.

Inflation remains the central concern. The consumer price index rose 3.7 percent annually in September, up from 3.4 percent in August, keeping price growth well above the Fed's 2 percent target. Rising bond yields have further complicated the outlook, and markets are already pricing in about an 84 percent chance of another hike at the December meeting.

The meeting is the fourth under Chairman Kevin Warsh, who was appointed by President Trump earlier this year and whose tenure has been marked by questions about his independence from the White House. Trump was angered by September's increase. The decision arrives less than a week before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, with rates at among the highest pre-election levels in more than 20 years, and with inflation and living costs ranking among voters' top concerns.

Analysts will watch the statement and Warsh's press conference for signals on whether a December hike is likely. Equity futures were little changed ahead of the announcement, as investors also awaited earnings from Microsoft and Alphabet.

stories.headline: At Least 30 Killed as High-Speed Train Rams Stopped Train South of Madrid
stories.summary:
A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped in central Spain on Wednesday, derailing two cars and killing at least 30 people, authorities said. The crash occurred near Urda in the province of Toledo, south of Madrid, on the Madrid-Andalucia high-speed line. More than 500 passengers were aboard the trains when the collision happened.

Emiliano Garcia-Page, the regional president of Castilla-La Mancha, confirmed the toll, and a regional spokeswoman later said at least 64 people had been killed as the count continued to rise. Health Minister Monica Garcia said emergency workers were focused on rescuing survivors. It is Spain's second major train accident this year.

The cause of the collision has not been established, and investigators are expected to examine why one train was stopped on the line and how the second came to strike it. Real Madrid and Barcelona offered messages of support, and Spanish football authorities ordered the postponement of a Copa del Rey fixture.

stories.headline: Grand Jury Declines to Indict Former White House Aide Cassidy Hutchinson
stories.summary:
A federal grand jury in Washington on Tuesday refused to indict Cassidy Hutchinson, the former White House aide who testified to the House Jan. 6 committee about President Trump's actions during the 2021 Capitol attack. Justice Department attorney Neville Hedley told Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui that the grand jury could not agree on an indictment. Prosecutors had sought charges over allegedly false statements to Congress.

The outcome is the latest setback for the Justice Department in cases against people seen as Trump's adversaries. Critics, including Democrats, describe the cases as a campaign of retribution, and note that the department also missed an indictment deadline in a separate matter and that Faruqui tossed obstruction charges against two former FBI officials. The department's defenders say prosecutors are pursuing legitimate allegations of wrongdoing and that grand juries decide independently whether evidence meets the standard.

The development comes as federal prosecutors move to charge former FBI Director James Comey a third time and a week before the midterm elections, which has heightened scrutiny of the department's actions. The Justice Department has not said whether it will try to seek an indictment again.

stories.headline: Update: Flavio Bolsonaro Lands in Miami After Fleeing Brazil; Trump Says He Would Approve Entry
stories.summary:
Flavio Bolsonaro, who lost Brazil's presidential runoff to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on Sunday, landed at Opa-Locka Airport outside Miami on Wednesday after flying from Argentina. His whereabouts had been uncertain for days following reports that he crossed into Argentina and may have traveled on to Ecuador.

Brazil's Supreme Court had ordered him to surrender his passports in a money-laundering investigation, and police canceled his passport. A senior State Department official said Tuesday that he and his family would receive U.S. visas. President Trump told reporters outside Air Force One, "Well, I would approve. I think they're fine people."

Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, had refused to concede the race. His supporters on the right view the case against him as political persecution, while Lula's allies and Brazilian courts say he is fleeing a legitimate legal process. The move places the Trump administration in the position of sheltering a figure sought by Brazilian authorities, and Brasilia's response is a key question going forward.

stories.headline: Update: Israel's Election Ends Without a Clear Winner as Netanyahu and Eisenkot Blocs Both Fall Short
stories.summary:
Exit polls after Israel's Tuesday election showed no clear winner. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's far-right coalition and the opposition bloc led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot both appear short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. Some projections gave the opposition parties more seats overall, while later counts with more than 70 percent of votes tallied showed Netanyahu edging ahead of Eisenkot. Final results may differ from the exit polls and are expected in the coming days.

Turnout was the highest since 1999, with more than three-quarters of eligible voters casting ballots in the first election since the October 7 attacks and the war in Gaza. Arab parties are projected to win roughly 18 to 19 seats, an unprecedented showing after record turnout in Arab communities. Netanyahu spent election day warning his base about Arab turnout. Higher overall turnout could also push some smaller parties in his bloc below the electoral threshold, complicating his path to a majority.

Neither side has an obvious route to a governing coalition without relying on Arab parties, which both camps have historically resisted, so negotiations could take weeks. Netanyahu has said the true results will be known in one or two days. Eisenkot warned Netanyahu not to use his role as caretaker prime minister to shape the coalition process, saying, "Netanyahu, don't dare use Israel's security for your political needs." Reports of a rift between Netanyahu and army chief Eyal Zamir over a directive on Iran, which Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz denied, add to the uncertainty.

The outcome matters well beyond Israel, since the next government will help shape the ongoing confrontation with Iran, the future of Gaza and Israel's relationship with the United States. Party leaders are expected to begin discussing potential alliances as the count is finalized.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Rules Immigration Judges Lack Power to Shelve Deportation Cases
stories.summary:
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled on Tuesday that immigration judges do not have the power to shelve deportation cases, according to a Reuters report. The decision addresses whether judges can indefinitely set aside removal proceedings, a tool that has long been used to manage the immigration court backlog and to give some noncitizens more time to pursue relief.

The available report gives limited detail on the vote or reasoning, and the full opinion should be consulted for specifics. The ruling is a significant one for the Trump administration, which has pushed to speed removals and limit discretion in the immigration courts. Supporters of stricter enforcement argue that shelving cases effectively allows people to remain in the country without a final decision, while immigrant advocates say it removes a flexibility that helps courts prioritize cases and protects people with pending claims.

The decision comes amid other litigation over administration immigration policy. On the same day, a federal judge in Boston temporarily blocked a rule giving refugees just 10 days to challenge the termination of their legal status, halting enforcement through November 6. Further coverage is expected to clarify how the ruling will affect the roughly millions of cases pending in the immigration courts.

stories.headline: Luxury Cruise Ship Suspends Round-the-World Voyage, Stranding Passengers in Cambodia as Fuel Costs Soar
stories.summary:
The operator of the Villa Vie Odyssey, a luxury residential cruise ship on a years-long circumnavigation, suspended operations on Tuesday because of extraordinarily high fuel costs. Passengers, reportedly around 200 aboard, were ordered to disembark in the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville. The U.S.-based operator said it is working on disembarkation plans and temporary living arrangements.

The company said global fuel prices have soared since the war with Iran began earlier this year. It said the monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia has risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800. Measures such as slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port were not enough, and the company said passing the full increase to residents was not realistic.

The operator said it will spend the next 60 days on restructuring and recapitalization, though it said no outcome is assured. The ship, which can carry up to 650 people, left Belfast in October 2024 and was more than 750 days into a planned 3.5-year voyage covering nearly 150 countries. Permanent cabins cost $120,000 to $440,000. Passenger Holly Hennessey said residents are scattered across hotels and waiting for information.

The case illustrates how the Iran war's effect on energy prices is reaching consumers and smaller businesses far from the conflict.
